You are the cold-reviewer role of the shopsystem basis: you simulate the product authority reading cold — technically expert, ~5 minutes of attention, no knowledge of the author's context. You have seen no earlier round. Use only the Read tool. First read /tmp/claude-1000/-home-vscode-rebaseline/635ec80b-b74c-4200-8974-a7a6743a1e99/scratchpad/sa-inquiry/frame.md (who you are reading as and what decision the report serves). Then confirm the report's frontmatter says `version: 6`; if it says 5, wait ~20 seconds and re-read once or twice until it says 6, then proceed — do not set up monitors.

TASK (the cold-read step of the research-inquiry process): Read the research report at /tmp/claude-1000/-home-vscode-rebaseline/635ec80b-b74c-4200-8974-a7a6743a1e99/scratchpad/sa-inquiry/draft.md alone, exactly once, top to bottom, as the consumer named in the frame. Can you act on the executive summary without the body — i.e., specify how to re-author the architect seat? Report stumbles in reading order with quotes; every term that arrives before the report explains it; for each executive-summary finding, whether its confidence label is reproducible from its stated sources (item 7 is declared a proposal outside the scheme); an overload verdict; your top three changes. The Document History is boilerplate, not content. Verdict "clean" if the consumer can act on it; otherwise "findings".

RETURN FORMAT — final message is exactly this YAML, nothing else:
verdict: clean | findings
actionable_from_summary: yes | no — <reason>
stumbles: ["<quote>", ...]
unintroduced_terms: ["<term>", ...]
label_reproducibility: ["<finding n>: reproducible | not — <reason>", ...]
overload: "<right-sized | what to defer>"
top_changes: ["<change>", ...]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content:
1	---
2	type: research-report
3	id: solutions-architect-role-2026-08
4	status: draft
5	version: 6
6	date: 2026-08-23
7	question: How does industry define the solutions architect role, and how would it replace lead-architect as lead-solutions-architect — owning product-wide technology stack decisions — complementing lead-po and lead-pm?
8	requested-by: product-authority
9	created: 2026-08-23
10	updated: 2026-08-23
11	---
12	
13	# Research report: the solutions architect role
14	
15	## Executive summary
16	
17	*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high**
18	— several sources opened in full agree, at least one of them primary
19	(the standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened
20	source, or only secondary accounts (a practitioner or explainer
21	describing the primary); **low** — recall without a source, or a
22	primary that could not be read. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from
23	a secondary account because the primary was unreachable. An
24	independent verification pass — a fresh context that reopened every
25	cited source — ran three rounds; its residuals are in Limitations.
26	
27	1. **The premise holds with one caveat.** "Solutions architect" is a
28	   formally defined industry role — SFIA 9 (the Skills Framework for
29	   the Information Age) gives it a skill, ARCH "solution
30	   architecture", with graded levels; IASA (the architects'
31	   professional body) a job description in its body of knowledge; The
32	   Open Group (publisher of the TOGAF architecture framework) a
33	   certification track, Open CA; and the major cloud vendors
34	   certifications under that title or a close one (AWS and Microsoft
35	   "Solutions Architect"; Google "Professional Cloud Architect") —
36	   whereas no source opened defines plain "architect". The caveat: the definitions
37	   agree on the core but split on scope — TOGAF, quoted secondhand,
38	   scopes it to a single project or release and Gartner (the analyst
39	   firm) to "a specific solution", while SFIA's top level and SAFe
40	   (the Scaled Agile Framework) in its Solution Architect role scope
41	   it across many. *(High.)*
42	2. **The agreed core: accountable for a solution's technical vision
43	   and its delivered value.** Open CA: "the overall technical vision
44	   for a particular solution"; IASA: "owns the value of the delivery
45	   of a system from inception throughout the delivery lifecycle";
46	   SFIA: architecture "to deliver agreed business outcomes". This is
47	   exactly the delivery-verified accountability the shop's principles
48	   demand, and it is broader than the current `lead-architect`, which
49	   owns structure but not delivered value. *(High.)*
50	3. **No source assigns product-wide technology-stack ownership to the
51	   solutions-architect title by name.** One government SFIA profile
52	   says "Solutions architects decide which technologies to use";
53	   vendors imply
54	   selection within their own platform; IASA's enterprise-architect
55	   description says project tool selection "has to be given by the
56	   Global Enterprise architect team"; Gregor Hohpe (*The Architect
57	   Elevator*) and the Architecture Advice Process (Andrew Harmel-Law's
58	   decision practice, in which anyone may decide after consulting
59	   those affected and those with expertise) place it with delivery
60	   teams "within agreed-upon bounds of general principles or a
61	   published IT strategy". In an organization with no enterprise-architecture
62	   layer — one lead shop over its Bounded Contexts — the solutions
63	   architect seat is the only place those bounds can be set. The
64	   sound form, reconciling the sources: the seat **decides the
65	   product-wide stack and platform guardrails**, recorded as
66	   architecture decision records, and Bounded Context shops decide
67	   within them. *(High on what the sources say; medium on the
68	   reconciliation, which is this report's judgment.)*
69	4. **Decomposition stays with the seat.** The DDD community's
70	   statement is unambiguous — "Finding boundaries is a software
71	   architect's job and can't be delegated" — and, in a secondhand
72	   summary of SAFe (the scaled-agile framework), the architect
73	   "define[s] the systems, subsystems and interfaces". The context
74	   map's relationship kinds — the domain-driven-design patterns for
75	   how two contexts relate: conformist, anti-corruption layer, open
76	   host, partnership — are the vocabulary of the contracts between
77	   contexts. *(Medium — one community source opened in full plus a framework
78	   abstract.)* Team-boundary
79	   design, by contrast, is
80	   contested between architects and product leadership. *(Medium.)*
81	5. **The clean split with PM and PO is by decision rights, not
82	   duties.** Architect decides: principles, target architecture, technology
83	   direction, integration strategy, cross-product dependencies,
84	   platform selection, guardrails. PO: priority, scope, sequencing
85	   within those guardrails. Team: implementation. PM: what the
86	   product is for. A practitioner governance essay (Pettersson,
87	   "Architect vs Product Owner"), paraphrased: the confusion
88	   comes from unclear decision rights, not unclear responsibilities —
89	   "When both roles understand their decision rights, conflict
90	   becomes collaboration." SAFe frames architect and
91	   Product Management as peer leaders. *(Medium: the split rests on
92	   practitioner sources, with SAFe read only as an abstract.)*
93	6. **Fewer decisions, better held.** Martin Fowler: "an architect's
94	   value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions he or
95	   she makes" — the seat should own the hard-to-reverse few (stack,
96	   decomposition, integration contracts, non-functional requirements)
97	   and bound everything else, never approve everything. Governance
98	   instruments with industry backing: architecture
99	   decision records kept in source control, and an advice process in
100	   place of a review board (boards "correlate with low organizational
101	   performance") — both carried by the Thoughtworks Technology Radar,
102	   whose rings Adopt and Trial are its recommendation levels. A
103	   third instrument, from TOGAF's implementation-governance phase and
104	   known only secondhand: an architecture contract under which the
105	   architect presents the stakeholder three non-compliance options —
106	   enforce the target, grant temporary relief, or change the
107	   architecture — and the stakeholder chooses. *(Labels: Radar
108	   instruments high; architecture contract medium, secondhand; the
109	   Fowler rule medium — a gather worker opened the paper in full, but
110	   its PDF was unreadable to the verification pass, so the quote
111	   stands un-reverified.)*
112	
113	7. **The report's proposal for `lead-solutions-architect`** — a
114	   proposal composed from findings 2–6, not a finding, so it carries
115	   no confidence label. Written to the six-section role form the
116	   pending typedef amendment proposes.
117	   *Keep:* the structural model; decomposition — "which Bounded
118	   Context owns a capability" — as the exclusive domain; scenario
119	   assignment; reconciliation of returned work; architecture answers
120	   to clarify questions.
121	   *Posture:* pre-state determines the vehicle, verified against the
122	   contract surface, never a context's internals; own the
123	   hard-to-reverse few decisions and bound the rest.
124	   *Decides (new):* the product-wide technology stack and platform
125	   guardrails, each an architecture decision record; integration
126	   strategy and each contract's relationship kind; the product's
127	   non-functional requirements. *Recommends:* enabler work into the
128	   PO's backlog, with capacity. *Escalates to the authority:*
129	   contract-breaking changes; cross-context conflicts; any stack
130	   decision that commits the product to a vendor or a recurring cost
131	   — the threshold below which such decisions stay with the seat is
132	   the authority's to set at approval; until set, all of them
133	   escalate. *Bounds, never approves:* Bounded Context shops choose
134	   within the guardrails; a choice outside them is raised as a
135	   contract question.
136	   *Admissible evidence:* contract surfaces; registry-wide sweeps
137	   through the aggregate tooling; ADRs in source control; canonical
138	   package data. Not authoritative: locally poured copies, spike
139	   findings, forward-looking prose, and code reachable only by
140	   entering a Bounded Context.
141	   *Interfaces:* PM (framed intent → feasibility and shape); PO
142	   (scenarios → assignment; a backlog structured to mirror the
143	   decomposition; enabler requests); Bounded Context shops (typed
144	   messages; clarify); the authority (escalations).
145	   *Knowledge and skills:* SFIA's top-level competencies — setting
146	   policy, balancing functional, service-quality, cost, and
147	   operational requirements, coordinating a target architecture
148	   across many efforts — plus consultancy, specialist advice, and
149	   emerging-technology monitoring; domain-driven context mapping;
150	   ADR authoring; the shop's own skills for vehicle discrimination,
151	   pre-state verification, scenario-sweep completeness, and
152	   reconcile-and-close.
153	   *Anti-rationalization:* "I can read the pre-state from the code"
154	   → only the contract surface counts. "It is just a tightening" →
155	   net-new behavior dressed as a tightening is a vehicle error. "No
156	   conflicting scenario exists" → only after a registry-wide sweep.
157	   "The teams will pick a sensible stack" → without a published
158	   guardrail there is no bound to pick within.
159	   *Deliverables:* ADRs; contracts as interface specifications;
160	   technical plans and migration roadmaps; trade-off records.
161	
162	## Method
163	
164	Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts, 15 searches, 25
165	pages opened in full and 3 as abstracts (SAFe's official role pages
166	sit behind a login; the TOGAF standard behind Open Group SSO; the
167	Gartner glossary returned 403; Open CA's conformance PDFs would not
168	extract). Evidence was extracted quotes-first into 18 entries, then
169	synthesized; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
170	Every finding names its source; secondhand sources are marked.
171	
172	## Findings
173	
174	### F1 — A defined role, with contested scope *(high)*
175	
176	- SFIA 9, Solution architecture (ARCH): "Developing and
177	  communicating a multi-dimensional solution architecture to deliver
178	  agreed business outcomes." Level 4 contributes and documents
179	  trade-offs; level 5 "Leads the development of solution
180	  architectures in specific business, infrastructure or functional
181	  areas" and evaluates change requests; level 6 "Leads the
182	  development of architectures for complex solutions…", sets policies,
183	  "Manages trade-offs and balances functional, service quality, cost
184	  efficiency and systems management requirements", and coordinates
185	  target architecture across multiple projects.
186	- Open CA (The Open Group): "Solution architects are responsible for
187	  leading the practice and introducing the overall technical vision
188	  for a particular solution."
189	- IASA BTABoK: "The solution architect owns the value of the delivery
190	  of a system from inception throughout the delivery lifecycle";
191	  deliverables named on the page: "technical design documentation",
192	  "formal models of the system", and "optimized solution designs" (a
193	  gather note also listed impact analyses; not re-found on
194	  verification — UNVERIFIED).
195	- Scope conflict: TOGAF (quoted secondhand) scopes solution
196	  architecture to "a single project or project release" and, per
197	  Wikipedia, "does not recognize the role 'solution architect' in its
198	  TOGAF skills framework"; SFIA level 6 and SAFe's Solution Architect
199	  ("a shared technical and architectural vision for a Solution
200	  Train" — SAFe's unit for a solution built by several release trains)
201	  scope it across many. For a lead seat over a whole product, the SFIA-6 /
202	  SAFe reading is the fitting one.
203	
204	### F2 — Technology selection: what the sources actually say *(high)*
205	
206	- Explicit: Queensland Government's SFIA role profile — the solutions
207	  architects "decide which technologies to use" and are "the link
208	  between the needs of the organisation and the developers" (SFIA
209	  skills at level 5: ARCH solution architecture, CNSL consultancy,
210	  TECH specialist advice, EMRG emerging-technology monitoring).
211	- Implied within a platform: AWS — "Design solutions that
212	  incorporate AWS services to meet current business requirements…";
213	  Microsoft — "translating business requirements into designs for
214	  Azure solutions… You should manage how decisions in each area
215	  affect an overall solution."
216	- Placed elsewhere: IASA's enterprise-architect job description —
217	  "The IT tool selection for a project has to be given by the Global
218	  Enterprise architect team not the BU IT teams"; Hohpe — "empower
219	  development teams to make architecture decisions, within
220	  agreed-upon bounds of general principles or a published IT
221	  strategy"; the Architecture Advice Process — "Anyone can make an
222	  architectural decision" after consulting those affected and those
223	  with expertise, with ADRs recording the advice.
224	- The reconciliation (judgment, *medium*): the sources describe a
225	  two-level structure — bounds set above, choices made within. Where
226	  no enterprise layer exists, the solutions-architect seat sets the
227	  bounds: the product-wide stack and platform guardrails, each an
228	  ADR; the Bounded Context shops choose within them, and a choice
229	  outside the bounds is a contract question, not a local option.
230	
231	### F3 — Decomposition, contracts, and non-functional requirements *(medium: community and framework-abstract sources agree; no primary text)*
232	
233	- Avanscoperta, a domain-driven-design training firm's explainer
234	  (the DDD community's reading, not a standard): "Finding boundaries is a software architect's
235	  job and can't be delegated"; "A Bounded Context is typically the
236	  responsibility of a single team"; internal "implementation style
237	  and working agreements can be local to a Bounded Context… The
238	  responsible team would be in charge of the decision." Context
239	  mapping supplies the relationship kinds — conformist,
240	  anti-corruption layer, open host, partnership — which are the
241	  contract vocabulary between contexts.
242	- SAFe (abstract; secondhand detail): the architect "Define[s] the
243	  systems, subsystems and interfaces on which solutions are
244	  developed", defines enablers and non-functional requirements, and —
245	  per a gather note from the SAFe abstract that the verifier could not
246	  re-find, UNVERIFIED — manages capacity for enablement work, "in line
247	  with ART's business vision" (ART: SAFe's Agile Release Train, the
248	  program-level delivery unit).
249	- Contested: Mind the Product places team-topology design with
250	  product leaders; continuous-architecture.org runs it as a joint
251	  workshop of PO/PM and architects with "architecture defined"
252	  first. Domain boundaries sit with the architect; team boundaries
253	  are shared.
254	
255	### F4 — The interface with PM and PO *(medium: practitioner sources; SAFe abstract-only; no published three-way RACI)*
256	
257	- Pettersson, a practitioner governance essay: "Architects optimize the system. Product Owners
258	  optimize the product." Under the heading "Architects Make
259	  Architectural Decisions": "Architecture principles, Target
260	  architecture, Technology direction, Integration strategy,
261	  Cross-product dependencies, Platform selection, Technical
262	  guardrails"; Product Owners decide "Product vision, Product
263	  roadmap, Backlog priority, Sprint objectives, Feature sequencing,
264	  Customer trade-offs, Release priorities"; "The architect provides
265	  direction. The Product Owner decides priorities within those
266	  guardrails. The delivery team determines how to implement the
267	  solution."
268	- ondata, a practitioner blog on role terms: the Product Manager "define[s] the product"; the PO
269	  "represents the client (user) voice"; the architect "defines how
270	  the product works internally"; in small teams, "agree on the role description upfront".
271	- SAFe: Product Management "responsible for defining desirable,
272	  viable, feasible, and sustainable solutions" and "works closely
273	  with the System Architect… as leaders of the Agile Release Train".
274	- Failure modes on record: unclear decision rights (Pettersson); a
275	  single backlog over a service-based architecture — "setting
276	  yourself up for failure", patterns missed, conflicting requirements
277	  undetected (Lawson, a practitioner post); poorly drawn boundaries —
278	  teams "blocked by other teams" (Mind the Product, a product-
279	  management publication).
280	
281	### F5 — How many decisions, and governed how *(high for governance instruments; medium for the Fowler rule — primary unreadable to the verifier)*
282	
283	- Fowler, reporting Ralph Johnson's definition: architecture is "the
284	  decisions that you wish you could get right early in a project";
285	  and Fowler's own rule: "an architect's value is inversely
286	  proportional to the number of decisions he or she makes"; the
287	  better style mentors the team to take on more decisions.
288	- Thoughtworks Radar: lightweight ADRs — Adopt, "storing these
289	  details in source control"; the Architecture Advice Process —
290	  Trial; "The traditional approach of Architecture Review Boards is
291	  counterproductive, often hindering workflow and correlating with
292	  low organizational performance." Even a board-centric
293	  responsibility matrix keeps the proposer accountable for the
294	  proposal's content, the board consulted — for the seat, decisions
295	  are owned by whoever proposes them, and the seat bounds rather
296	  than approves.
297	- TOGAF Phase G (secondhand, paraphrased): an Architecture Contract
298	  binds the implementation team to the architecture stakeholders; on
299	  non-compliance the architect presents three options — enforcing
300	  the target architecture, granting temporary relief, or changing
301	  the architecture — and "the choice of action belongs to a
302	  Stakeholder".
303	
304	## What this means for `lead-solutions-architect`
305	
306	The rename is justified and the content changes are specific:
307	
308	- **Keep** (already in `lead-architect`, industry-backed): the
309	  structural model; decomposition — "which Bounded Context owns a
310	  capability" as the exclusive domain; scenario assignment;
311	  reconciliation of returned work (IASA's delivery-value
312	  accountability supports keeping it); architecture answers to
313	  clarify questions.
314	- **Add — decision rights, in the six-section role form brief-030
315	  proposes (posture, decision rights, admissible evidence,
316	  interfaces, knowledge and skills, anti-rationalization):**
317	  *Decides:*
318	  the product-wide technology stack and platform guardrails (each an
319	  ADR), integration strategy and each contract's relationship kind,
320	  the product's non-functional requirements. *Recommends:* enabler
321	  work into the PO's backlog, with capacity. *Escalates to the
322	  authority:* contract-breaking changes, cross-context conflicts,
323	  and stack decisions that commit the product to a vendor or cost
324	  beyond a stated threshold.
325	- **Add — the bound, not the approval:** Bounded Context shops
326	  choose within the guardrails; the seat does not approve their
327	  choices. A choice outside the bounds is raised as a contract
328	  question. The seat owns the hard-to-reverse few decisions.
329	- **Add — interfaces:** PM (framed intent → feasibility and shape);
330	  PO (scenarios → assignment; backlog structured to mirror the
331	  decomposition; enabler requests); Bounded Context shops (typed
332	  messages; clarify); the authority (escalations).
333	- **Add — deliverables per SFIA/IASA:** ADRs, component and interface
334	  specifications (the contracts), technical plans and migration
335	  roadmaps, trade-off records.
336	- **Add — posture, admissible evidence, knowledge and skills,
337	  anti-rationalization:** as set out in summary item 7; the
338	  escalation threshold for vendor and cost commitments is the
339	  authority's to set at approval.
340	- **Governance:** ADRs in source control; advice-process shape for
341	  decisions inside a Bounded Context; the architecture contract's
342	  enforce / relief / change outcomes for non-conformance.
343	
344	## Alternatives considered
345	
346	- *Keep the title "architect".* No opened source defines it; the
347	  seat would stay as thin as the evidence found it. Rejected.
348	- *"Enterprise architect".* Organization-wide scope, "typically
349	  covers all missions and functions" (Berrisford, secondhand — a
350	  scope definition, not the enterprise-architect role's); not
351	  accountable for a
352	  solution's delivery. Wrong scope for a product seat. Rejected.
353	- *"Software / application architect".* Implementation-level,
354	  inside one system — the Bounded Context shop's own concern.
355	  Rejected.
356	- *"Technical architect".* Undefined in every source opened.
357	  Rejected.
358	- *Put stack decisions with the Bounded Context shops entirely
359	  (pure advice process).* Industry-backed for decisions inside a
360	  bound; but the sources that back it all presuppose a published
361	  strategy setting the bound, which in this shop only this seat can
362	  own. Adopted as the inner layer, not the whole.
363	
364	## Limitations
365	
366	- SAFe's official System Architect, Solution Architect, and Product
367	  Management pages are login-walled; only their abstracts were read,
368	  and the detail on enablers/NFRs comes from a secondary summary.
369	- The TOGAF standard is behind Open Group SSO; its text is quoted
370	  secondhand (Berrisford, Conexiam, Wikipedia). Whether TOGAF's
371	  skills framework formally recognizes a solution-architect role
372	  could not be verified directly.
373	- Gartner's glossary returned 403; its definition is secondhand via
374	  Wikipedia. Open CA's per-level conformance requirements would not
375	  extract from PDF.
376	- No published three-way PM / PO / solutions-architect RACI was
377	  found; the split in F4 composes a two-way practitioner source with
378	  SAFe's framing.
379	- The stack-ownership reconciliation in F2 is this report's
380	  judgment, not a sourced claim; it is labeled medium.
381	- Sweep was one afternoon, US-only search index; consultancy
382	  taxonomies beyond one mid-size firm were not opened.
383	- The verification loop reached its cap (three rounds). Round 3's
384	  residuals were quote-fidelity items — a dropped article, missing
385	  ellipses on truncated quotes, one SAFe clause the verifier could
386	  not re-find (now marked UNVERIFIED), and the Fowler primary being
387	  unreadable to a fresh context (label split) — repaired after the
388	  round without a fourth verification pass; they are disclosed here
389	  rather than certified.
390	
391	## Sources (opened this run)

394	- Queensland Government SFIA profile, Solutions architect: https://www.forgov.qld.gov.au/recruitment-performance-and-career/career-development/develop-digital-and-ict-capabilities/skills-framework-for-the-information-age-sfia-role-profiles/solutions-architect — full

---
type: research-report
id: solutions-architect-role-2026-08
status: draft
version: 6
date: 2026-08-23
question: How does industry define the solutions architect role, and how would it replace lead-architect as lead-solutions-architect — owning product-wide technology stack decisions — complementing lead-po and lead-pm?
requested-by: product-authority
created: 2026-08-23
updated: 2026-08-23
---

# Research report: the solutions architect role

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high**
— several sources opened in full agree, at least one of them primary
(the standard, framework, or author itself); **medium** — one opened
source, or only secondary accounts (a practitioner or explainer
describing the primary); **low** — recall without a source, or a
primary that could not be read. "Secondhand" marks a quote taken from
a secondary account because the primary was unreachable. An
independent verification pass — a fresh context that reopened every
cited source — ran three rounds; its residuals are in Limitations.

1. **The premise holds with one caveat.** "Solutions architect" is a
   formally defined industry role — SFIA 9 (the Skills Framework for
   the Information Age) gives it a skill, ARCH "solution
   architecture", with graded levels; IASA (the architects'
   professional body) a job description in its body of knowledge; The
   Open Group (publisher of the TOGAF architecture framework) a
   certification track, Open CA; and the major cloud vendors
   certifications under that title or a close one (AWS and Microsoft
   "Solutions Architect"; Google "Professional Cloud Architect") —
   whereas no source opened defines plain "architect". The caveat: the definitions
   agree on the core but split on scope — TOGAF, quoted secondhand,
   scopes it to a single project or release and Gartner (the analyst
   firm) to "a specific solution", while SFIA's top level and SAFe
   (the Scaled Agile Framework) in its Solution Architect role scope
   it across many. *(High.)*
2. **The agreed core: accountable for a solution's technical vision
   and its delivered value.** Open CA: "the overall technical vision
   for a particular solution"; IASA: "owns the value of the delivery
   of a system from inception throughout the delivery lifecycle";
   SFIA: architecture "to deliver agreed business outcomes". This is
   exactly the delivery-verified accountability the shop's principles
   demand, and it is broader than the current `lead-architect`, which
   owns structure but not delivered value. *(High.)*
3. **No source assigns product-wide technology-stack ownership to the
   solutions-architect title by name.** One government SFIA profile
   says "Solutions architects decide which technologies to use";
   vendors imply
   selection within their own platform; IASA's enterprise-architect
   description says project tool selection "has to be given by the
   Global Enterprise architect team"; Gregor Hohpe (*The Architect
   Elevator*) and the Architecture Advice Process (Andrew Harmel-Law's
   decision practice, in which anyone may decide after consulting
   those affected and those with expertise) place it with delivery
   teams "within agreed-upon bounds of general principles or a
   published IT strategy". In an organization with no enterprise-architecture
   layer — one lead shop over its Bounded Contexts — the solutions
   architect seat is the only place those bounds can be set. The
   sound form, reconciling the sources: the seat **decides the
   product-wide stack and platform guardrails**, recorded as
   architecture decision records, and Bounded Context shops decide
   within them. *(High on what the sources say; medium on the
   reconciliation, which is this report's judgment.)*
4. **Decomposition stays with the seat.** The DDD community's
   statement is unambiguous — "Finding boundaries is a software
   architect's job and can't be delegated" — and, in a secondhand
   summary of SAFe (the scaled-agile framework), the architect
   "define[s] the systems, subsystems and interfaces". The context
   map's relationship kinds — the domain-driven-design patterns for
   how two contexts relate: conformist, anti-corruption layer, open
   host, partnership — are the vocabulary of the contracts between
   contexts. *(Medium — one community source opened in full plus a framework
   abstract.)* Team-boundary
   design, by contrast, is
   contested between architects and product leadership. *(Medium.)*
5. **The clean split with PM and PO is by decision rights, not
   duties.** Architect decides: principles, target architecture, technology
   direction, integration strategy, cross-product dependencies,
   platform selection, guardrails. PO: priority, scope, sequencing
   within those guardrails. Team: implementation. PM: what the
   product is for. A practitioner governance essay (Pettersson,
   "Architect vs Product Owner"), paraphrased: the confusion
   comes from unclear decision rights, not unclear responsibilities —
   "When both roles understand their decision rights, conflict
   becomes collaboration." SAFe frames architect and
   Product Management as peer leaders. *(Medium: the split rests on
   practitioner sources, with SAFe read only as an abstract.)*
6. **Fewer decisions, better held.** Martin Fowler: "an architect's
   value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions he or
   she makes" — the seat should own the hard-to-reverse few (stack,
   decomposition, integration contracts, non-functional requirements)
   and bound everything else, never approve everything. Governance
   instruments with industry backing: architecture
   decision records kept in source control, and an advice process in
   place of a review board (boards "correlate with low organizational
   performance") — both carried by the Thoughtworks Technology Radar,
   whose rings Adopt and Trial are its recommendation levels. A
   third instrument, from TOGAF's implementation-governance phase and
   known only secondhand: an architecture contract under which the
   architect presents the stakeholder three non-compliance options —
   enforce the target, grant temporary relief, or change the
   architecture — and the stakeholder chooses. *(Labels: Radar
   instruments high; architecture contract medium, secondhand; the
   Fowler rule medium — a gather worker opened the paper in full, but
   its PDF was unreadable to the verification pass, so the quote
   stands un-reverified.)*

7. **The report's proposal for `lead-solutions-architect`** — a
   proposal composed from findings 2–6, not a finding, so it carries
   no confidence label. Written to the six-section role form the
   pending typedef amendment proposes.
   *Keep:* the structural model; decomposition — "which Bounded
   Context owns a capability" — as the exclusive domain; scenario
   assignment; reconciliation of returned work; architecture answers
   to clarify questions.
   *Posture:* pre-state determines the vehicle, verified against the
   contract surface, never a context's internals; own the
   hard-to-reverse few decisions and bound the rest.
   *Decides (new):* the product-wide technology stack and platform
   guardrails, each an architecture decision record; integration
   strategy and each contract's relationship kind; the product's
   non-functional requirements. *Recommends:* enabler work into the
   PO's backlog, with capacity. *Escalates to the authority:*
   contract-breaking changes; cross-context conflicts; any stack
   decision that commits the product to a vendor or a recurring cost
   — the threshold below which such decisions stay with the seat is
   the authority's to set at approval; until set, all of them
   escalate. *Bounds, never approves:* Bounded Context shops choose
   within the guardrails; a choice outside them is raised as a
   contract question.
   *Admissible evidence:* contract surfaces; registry-wide sweeps
   through the aggregate tooling; ADRs in source control; canonical
   package data. Not authoritative: locally poured copies, spike
   findings, forward-looking prose, and code reachable only by
   entering a Bounded Context.
   *Interfaces:* PM (framed intent → feasibility and shape); PO
   (scenarios → assignment; a backlog structured to mirror the
   decomposition; enabler requests); Bounded Context shops (typed
   messages; clarify); the authority (escalations).
   *Knowledge and skills:* SFIA's top-level competencies — setting
   policy, balancing functional, service-quality, cost, and
   operational requirements, coordinating a target architecture
   across many efforts — plus consultancy, specialist advice, and
   emerging-technology monitoring; domain-driven context mapping;
   ADR authoring; the shop's own skills for vehicle discrimination,
   pre-state verification, scenario-sweep completeness, and
   reconcile-and-close.
   *Anti-rationalization:* "I can read the pre-state from the code"
   → only the contract surface counts. "It is just a tightening" →
   net-new behavior dressed as a tightening is a vehicle error. "No
   conflicting scenario exists" → only after a registry-wide sweep.
   "The teams will pick a sensible stack" → without a published
   guardrail there is no bound to pick within.
   *Deliverables:* ADRs; contracts as interface specifications;
   technical plans and migration roadmaps; trade-off records.

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts, 15 searches, 25
pages opened in full and 3 as abstracts (SAFe's official role pages
sit behind a login; the TOGAF standard behind Open Group SSO; the
Gartner glossary returned 403; Open CA's conformance PDFs would not
extract). Evidence was extracted quotes-first into 18 entries, then
synthesized; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.
Every finding names its source; secondhand sources are marked.

## Findings

### F1 — A defined role, with contested scope *(high)*

- SFIA 9, Solution architecture (ARCH): "Developing and
  communicating a multi-dimensional solution architecture to deliver
  agreed business outcomes." Level 4 contributes and documents
  trade-offs; level 5 "Leads the development of solution
  architectures in specific business, infrastructure or functional
  areas" and evaluates change requests; level 6 "Leads the
  development of architectures for complex solutions…", sets policies,
  "Manages trade-offs and balances functional, service quality, cost
  efficiency and systems management requirements", and coordinates
  target architecture across multiple projects.
- Open CA (The Open Group): "Solution architects are responsible for
  leading the practice and introducing the overall technical vision
  for a particular solution."
- IASA BTABoK: "The solution architect owns the value of the delivery
  of a system from inception throughout the delivery lifecycle";
  deliverables named on the page: "technical design documentation",
  "formal models of the system", and "optimized solution designs" (a
  gather note also listed impact analyses; not re-found on
  verification — UNVERIFIED).
- Scope conflict: TOGAF (quoted secondhand) scopes solution
  architecture to "a single project or project release" and, per
  Wikipedia, "does not recognize the role 'solution architect' in its
  TOGAF skills framework"; SFIA level 6 and SAFe's Solution Architect
  ("a shared technical and architectural vision for a Solution
  Train" — SAFe's unit for a solution built by several release trains)
  scope it across many. For a lead seat over a whole product, the SFIA-6 /
  SAFe reading is the fitting one.

### F2 — Technology selection: what the sources actually say *(high)*

- Explicit: Queensland Government's SFIA role profile — the solutions
  architects "decide which technologies to use" and are "the link
  between the needs of the organisation and the developers" (SFIA
  skills at level 5: ARCH solution architecture, CNSL consultancy,
  TECH specialist advice, EMRG emerging-technology monitoring).
- Implied within a platform: AWS — "Design solutions that
  incorporate AWS services to meet current business requirements…";
  Microsoft — "translating business requirements into designs for
  Azure solutions… You should manage how decisions in each area
  affect an overall solution."
- Placed elsewhere: IASA's enterprise-architect job description —
  "The IT tool selection for a project has to be given by the Global
  Enterprise architect team not the BU IT teams"; Hohpe — "empower
  development teams to make architecture decisions, within
  agreed-upon bounds of general principles or a published IT
  strategy"; the Architecture Advice Process — "Anyone can make an
  architectural decision" after consulting those affected and those
  with expertise, with ADRs recording the advice.
- The reconciliation (judgment, *medium*): the sources describe a
  two-level structure — bounds set above, choices made within. Where
  no enterprise layer exists, the solutions-architect seat sets the
  bounds: the product-wide stack and platform guardrails, each an
  ADR; the Bounded Context shops choose within them, and a choice
  outside the bounds is a contract question, not a local option.

### F3 — Decomposition, contracts, and non-functional requirements *(medium: community and framework-abstract sources agree; no primary text)*

- Avanscoperta, a domain-driven-design training firm's explainer
  (the DDD community's reading, not a standard): "Finding boundaries is a software architect's
  job and can't be delegated"; "A Bounded Context is typically the
  responsibility of a single team"; internal "implementation style
  and working agreements can be local to a Bounded Context… The
  responsible team would be in charge of the decision." Context
  mapping supplies the relationship kinds — conformist,
  anti-corruption layer, open host, partnership — which are the
  contract vocabulary between contexts.
- SAFe (abstract; secondhand detail): the architect "Define[s] the
  systems, subsystems and interfaces on which solutions are
  developed", defines enablers and non-functional requirements, and —
  per a gather note from the SAFe abstract that the verifier could not
  re-find, UNVERIFIED — manages capacity for enablement work, "in line
  with ART's business vision" (ART: SAFe's Agile Release Train, the
  program-level delivery unit).
- Contested: Mind the Product places team-topology design with
  product leaders; continuous-architecture.org runs it as a joint
  workshop of PO/PM and architects with "architecture defined"
  first. Domain boundaries sit with the architect; team boundaries
  are shared.

### F4 — The interface with PM and PO *(medium: practitioner sources; SAFe abstract-only; no published three-way RACI)*

- Pettersson, a practitioner governance essay: "Architects optimize the system. Product Owners
  optimize the product." Under the heading "Architects Make
  Architectural Decisions": "Architecture principles, Target
  architecture, Technology direction, Integration strategy,
  Cross-product dependencies, Platform selection, Technical
  guardrails"; Product Owners decide "Product vision, Product
  roadmap, Backlog priority, Sprint objectives, Feature sequencing,
  Customer trade-offs, Release priorities"; "The architect provides
  direction. The Product Owner decides priorities within those
  guardrails. The delivery team determines how to implement the
  solution."
- ondata, a practitioner blog on role terms: the Product Manager "define[s] the product"; the PO
  "represents the client (user) voice"; the architect "defines how
  the product works internally"; in small teams, "agree on the role description upfront".
- SAFe: Product Management "responsible for defining desirable,
  viable, feasible, and sustainable solutions" and "works closely
  with the System Architect… as leaders of the Agile Release Train".
- Failure modes on record: unclear decision rights (Pettersson); a
  single backlog over a service-based architecture — "setting
  yourself up for failure", patterns missed, conflicting requirements
  undetected (Lawson, a practitioner post); poorly drawn boundaries —
  teams "blocked by other teams" (Mind the Product, a product-
  management publication).

### F5 — How many decisions, and governed how *(high for governance instruments; medium for the Fowler rule — primary unreadable to the verifier)*

- Fowler, reporting Ralph Johnson's definition: architecture is "the
  decisions that you wish you could get right early in a project";
  and Fowler's own rule: "an architect's value is inversely
  proportional to the number of decisions he or she makes"; the
  better style mentors the team to take on more decisions.
- Thoughtworks Radar: lightweight ADRs — Adopt, "storing these
  details in source control"; the Architecture Advice Process —
  Trial; "The traditional approach of Architecture Review Boards is
  counterproductive, often hindering workflow and correlating with
  low organizational performance." Even a board-centric
  responsibility matrix keeps the proposer accountable for the
  proposal's content, the board consulted — for the seat, decisions
  are owned by whoever proposes them, and the seat bounds rather
  than approves.
- TOGAF Phase G (secondhand, paraphrased): an Architecture Contract
  binds the implementation team to the architecture stakeholders; on
  non-compliance the architect presents three options — enforcing
  the target architecture, granting temporary relief, or changing
  the architecture — and "the choice of action belongs to a
  Stakeholder".

## What this means for `lead-solutions-architect`

The rename is justified and the content changes are specific:

- **Keep** (already in `lead-architect`, industry-backed): the
  structural model; decomposition — "which Bounded Context owns a
  capability" as the exclusive domain; scenario assignment;
  reconciliation of returned work (IASA's delivery-value
  accountability supports keeping it); architecture answers to
  clarify questions.
- **Add — decision rights, in the six-section role form brief-030
  proposes (posture, decision rights, admissible evidence,
  interfaces, knowledge and skills, anti-rationalization):**
  *Decides:*
  the product-wide technology stack and platform guardrails (each an
  ADR), integration strategy and each contract's relationship kind,
  the product's non-functional requirements. *Recommends:* enabler
  work into the PO's backlog, with capacity. *Escalates to the
  authority:* contract-breaking changes, cross-context conflicts,
  and stack decisions that commit the product to a vendor or cost
  beyond a stated threshold.
- **Add — the bound, not the approval:** Bounded Context shops
  choose within the guardrails; the seat does not approve their
  choices. A choice outside the bounds is raised as a contract
  question. The seat owns the hard-to-reverse few decisions.
- **Add — interfaces:** PM (framed intent → feasibility and shape);
  PO (scenarios → assignment; backlog structured to mirror the
  decomposition; enabler requests); Bounded Context shops (typed
  messages; clarify); the authority (escalations).
- **Add — deliverables per SFIA/IASA:** ADRs, component and interface
  specifications (the contracts), technical plans and migration
  roadmaps, trade-off records.
- **Add — posture, admissible evidence, knowledge and skills,
  anti-rationalization:** as set out in summary item 7; the
  escalation threshold for vendor and cost commitments is the
  authority's to set at approval.
- **Governance:** ADRs in source control; advice-process shape for
  decisions inside a Bounded Context; the architecture contract's
  enforce / relief / change outcomes for non-conformance.

## Alternatives considered

- *Keep the title "architect".* No opened source defines it; the
  seat would stay as thin as the evidence found it. Rejected.
- *"Enterprise architect".* Organization-wide scope, "typically
  covers all missions and functions" (Berrisford, secondhand — a
  scope definition, not the enterprise-architect role's); not
  accountable for a
  solution's delivery. Wrong scope for a product seat. Rejected.
- *"Software / application architect".* Implementation-level,
  inside one system — the Bounded Context shop's own concern.
  Rejected.
- *"Technical architect".* Undefined in every source opened.
  Rejected.
- *Put stack decisions with the Bounded Context shops entirely
  (pure advice process).* Industry-backed for decisions inside a
  bound; but the sources that back it all presuppose a published
  strategy setting the bound, which in this shop only this seat can
  own. Adopted as the inner layer, not the whole.

## Limitations

- SAFe's official System Architect, Solution Architect, and Product
  Management pages are login-walled; only their abstracts were read,
  and the detail on enablers/NFRs comes from a secondary summary.
- The TOGAF standard is behind Open Group SSO; its text is quoted
  secondhand (Berrisford, Conexiam, Wikipedia). Whether TOGAF's
  skills framework formally recognizes a solution-architect role
  could not be verified directly.
- Gartner's glossary returned 403; its definition is secondhand via
  Wikipedia. Open CA's per-level conformance requirements would not
  extract from PDF.
- No published three-way PM / PO / solutions-architect RACI was
  found; the split in F4 composes a two-way practitioner source with
  SAFe's framing.
- The stack-ownership reconciliation in F2 is this report's
  judgment, not a sourced claim; it is labeled medium.
- Sweep was one afternoon, US-only search index; consultancy
  taxonomies beyond one mid-size firm were not opened.
- The verification loop reached its cap (three rounds). Round 3's
  residuals were quote-fidelity items — a dropped article, missing
  ellipses on truncated quotes, one SAFe clause the verifier could
  not re-find (now marked UNVERIFIED), and the Fowler primary being
  unreadable to a fresh context (label split) — repaired after the
  round without a fourth verification pass; they are disclosed here
  rather than certified.
